explain.say: You are in a new city, hungry. One food stall has a long queue; the other is empty. Which do you pick? Most of us pick the queue! Look at the board. This is Hiro in Osaka, Japan, trying to choose a ramen stall.

explain.say: See the second picture? One stall has a long queue. Hiro thinks, all those people must know something. When we are unsure, we copy what others do. Psychologists call this social proof: other people's actions act like proof of what is right. Where have you copied a crowd?

explain.say: Look at the third picture. Hiro joins the queue. Often social proof is useful: if everyone runs from a fire, running too is smart, and locals often know the best food. Copying helped early humans learn fast. When is copying others a good idea?

explain.say: Now see the fourth picture. The ramen is just OK. The stall was busy only because it was next to the station! Social proof can trick us: people may all be copying each other, with nobody really knowing. Adverts use this when they say millions love it. Have you seen an advert like that?

faq.a: Social proof is our habit of copying what other people do, especially when we are unsure, because their choices seem like proof of what is right. Psychologist Robert Cialdini made the term famous in 1984.
asks: Tell me about two food stalls

faq.q: Why do we copy other people when we are unsure?
faq.a: When we do not know what to do, other people's actions give us information. Copying them is a quick shortcut that often works, so our brains rely on it.
asks: Why do people follow the crowd?

faq.a: It helps when others really know more than you, like locals choosing food, or everyone leaving a building during an alarm. For early humans, copying others was a fast way to learn what was safe.
asks: Tell me about joins the queue

faq.q: How can social proof trick us?
faq.a: Sometimes everyone is copying everyone else and nobody really knows. Companies also use it with fake reviews, view counts and "best seller" labels to push us to buy.
asks: Tell me about not so special
How do adverts use social proof?

faq.q: How can I avoid being fooled by social proof?
faq.a: Treat the crowd as a clue, not the answer. Ask why something is popular, check real information, and think about whether it suits you.
asks: How do I think for myself?

facts: Robert Cialdini described social proof as one of six main principles of persuasion in his 1984 book "Influence".
In a 1969 New York study (Milgram and others), when 15 people stood staring up at a building, about 40 percent of passers-by stopped and looked up too.

quiz.say: You see a video with millions of views and decide it must be good. Which idea is this?
quiz.show: Thinking it is good because millions watched is…
quiz.why: Using other people's choices as proof of what is good is social proof.

wrong.1: Equity is about giving people what they need for fairness.
wrong.2: A tradition is a custom passed down over years.

quiz.say: When is following the crowd a sensible choice?
quiz.show: Following the crowd makes sense when…

options.show: An advert says millions love it
options.say: An advert says millions love it

options.show: Everyone leaves calmly during a fire alarm
options.say: Everyone leaves calmly during a fire alarm

options.show: Everyone copies each other with no reason
options.say: Everyone copies each other with no reason

quiz.why: In an alarm, others likely have good information and following keeps you safe.

wrong.0: Adverts use social proof to sell; check for yourself.
wrong.2: If nobody knows why, the crowd gives you no real information.
